newsitem.title: USA: Continental jet fuel hedges pay off in Q3.
newsitem.headline: Continental jet fuel hedges pay off in Q3.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc, hedging all of its jet fuel costs in the midst of a sharp four-month price spike, is currently the toast of the airline industry, which is facing potential hikes in fares.
"We've been successful with our hedging and it's been very beneficial to us," said Sarah Anthony, spokeswoman with Houston-based Continental.
Analysts said Continental has done a better job than the rest of the U.S. airline industry in controlling its exposure to the 40 percent rise in fuel costs since June.
Continental's third quarter fuel costs rose by 17.3 percent from the prior year third quarter, compared to 23 percent for the whole U.S. industry, said Lehman Brothers airline analyst Brian Harris.
"Obviously, they're getting a significant benefit," Harris said, "It's certainly worked this quarter."

At a time when spot jet fuel prices are reaching about 72 cents per gallon in New York Harbor, Continental's hedging traders have locked in jet fuel prices in the low 60s through the 1997 first quarter, roughly for the duration of the heating oil season in the populous Northeast.
That's about 16 percent below current prices, which have leaped to 70 cents a gallon since early summer and could well go far higher according to worried industry executives.
Jet fuel prices are pegged to heating oil, which has spiked sharply due to concerns over the lowest domestic inventories in a generation on the cusp of the peak winter demand period.

Hedging, or price risk management strategies, thus often involve buying or selling heating oil futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange, though tailor-made over-the-counter options and swaps can also help manage risk, sources said.
According to aviation industry data, jet fuel accounts for up to 15 percent of total airline expenses.
Prices, now their highest in six years, have already forced British Airways Plc to raise its published European fares by 2.5 percent, the carrier said Wednesday.
The biggest U.S. carrier, AMR Corp's American Airlines, said it will match BA's fare hike for its flights originating from the United Kingdom, but not from the U.S.
Other U.S. carriers declined to discuss future fare strategies, but said the rise in fuel costs has left them worried that prices may not have yet peaked.
"It is fair to say the level of jet fuel prices continues to be a problem and will probably be worse in the winter," said Tim Smith, spokesman at Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR.
Smith said American now hedges around 15 to 20 percent of its fuel costs, and might hedge more in the future.
Smith did not elaborate, but a top AMR executive told reporters in a telephone conference Wednesday that American has hedged a portion of its jet fuel costs for material needed 12 to 18 months away.
Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines declined to disclose details of its hedging program, but acknowledged it is now "looking at it" after its own jet fuel costs jumped about 20 percent this year.
"Each one cent increase in jet fuel costs translates into $25 million in extra costs each year," said Delta spokeswoman Kimberly King.

An aggravating factor, analysts noted, was the re-imposition last October of a 4.3-cents-per-gallon federal tax on jet fuel, a hefty sum but one which pales in comparison to the recent summer upswing in fuel costs.

Oil traders say Continental has been a hedging winner this time around, but noted it is an inherently risky activity. If the market were to turn sharply lower, they cautioned, Continental's hedging stance could quickly become a liability.
"There are no guarantees. The first time Continental did this, they had their heads handed to them," a East Coast jet fuel trader said.
